title: What are the functional and clinical characteristics shared by fibromyalgia and low back pain? A scoping review
authors: Bastien Couëpel; Mathieu Tremblay; Marjorie Bernier; Jacques Abboud; Martin Descarreaux
pain_condition_detail: Fibromyalgia and chronic primary low back pain
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' once in the abstract as a descriptor of burden. It does not define the model, cite a source, or use it to structure the review. The review is organized around pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes without invoking the BPS model analytically.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper asserts that psychological factors (catastrophizing, depression, anxiety) contribute to central sensitization, but no pathway or mechanism is specified. No integration between psychological and social, biological and social, or triadic domains is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' once but does not define it, cite a source, or use it to structure the review
conceptual_tensions_2: Psychological domain is elaborated with multiple constructs and instruments, but social domain is limited to one mention of social support
conceptual_tensions_3: Directional claims (e.g., catastrophizing contributes to central sensitization) are made without specifying a pathway or mechanism
additional_observations_1: The review compares FM and LBP on pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes but does not integrate these domains into a biopsychosocial account
additional_observations_2: The paper identifies methodological heterogeneity in definitions and instruments as a limitation, which is relevant to operationalization of constructs
synthesis_note: This scoping review compares FM and LBP on pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes. It uses 'biopsychosocial' once in the abstract without definition or integration. Psychological domain is elaborated; social domain is minimal. No triadic integration is proposed. The paper contributes to the question by showing how BPS language can be tokenistic even in a review that compares two chronic pain conditions.
coding_rationale: Typology is pseudo_bps because BPS label is used but social domain is minimal and no integration is present. Triadic integration is none because domains are listed in parallel. Psychological domain is elaborated with multiple constructs and instruments.

title: What are the functional and clinical characteristics shared by fibromyalgia and low back pain? A scoping review
authors: Bastien Couëpel; Mathieu Tremblay; Marjorie Bernier; Jacques Abboud; Martin Descarreaux
pain_condition_detail: fibromyalgia and chronic primary/non-specific low back pain
context_note: Included studies covered multiple countries; review restricted to English/French publications and three databases.
bps_operationalization_summary: BPS label is used to frame burden and organize comparison across pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes; the review does not define or model interactions among domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes psychological symptoms may contribute to central sensitization, central sensitization may predict widespread pain, and the relation with widespread pain may be bidirectional. No social-domain pathway is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses biopsychosocial burden while leaving the model undefined and unmechanized
conceptual_tensions_2: LBP definitions are inconsistent across included studies
conceptual_tensions_3: ACR criteria differ across studies and may select more severe FM cases
conceptual_tensions_4: Measurement heterogeneity and missing minimal clinically important differences limit synthesis
conceptual_tensions_5: The proposed psychological-to-widespread-pain pathway is explicitly bidirectional and unknown
additional_observations_1: No formal risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of included studies is reported
additional_observations_2: Included study designs were mostly cross-sectional, limiting claims about progression from LBP to FM
additional_observations_3: The search was restricted to English/French publications and three databases
additional_observations_4: The social domain appears mainly as social support and socioeconomic descriptors, not as a modeled determinant
synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a comparative framework rather than an integrated explanatory model. Biological and psychological mechanisms are discussed, especially central sensitization and affect/cognition, but social content is reduced to socioeconomic context and social support.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic; triadic integration is partial because social factors are not tied into the mechanism. Typology is multifactorial.

title: What are the functional and clinical characteristics shared by fibromyalgia and low back pain? A scoping review
authors: Bastien Couëpel; Mathieu Tremblay; Marjorie Bernier; Jacques Abboud; Martin Descarreaux
pain_condition_detail: fibromyalgia and chronic low back pain
bps_operationalization_summary: Organizes the review scope around pain-related, physiological and psychological characteristics without integrating domains. BPS label appears as descriptor of burden and as justification for multi-characteristic analysis, but domains are treated as separate outcome categories.
conceptual_tensions_1: Tension between BPS label usage and complete absence of social domain analysis
conceptual_tensions_2: Discrepancy between claimed BPS framework and actual domain separation in methodology
additional_observations_1: Review focuses exclusively on biological and psychological factors with no social determinants or contextual factors
additional_observations_2: BPS label appears primarily as descriptor of burden rather than as analytical framework
additional_observations_3: Central sensitization serves as biological mechanism linking FM and LBP conditions
additional_observations_4: Psychological factors (catastrophizing, depression, anxiety) positioned as determinants of central sensitization
synthesis_note: This scoping review examines similarities and differences between fibromyalgia and low back pain across biological (central sensitization, pain sensitivity, fMRI patterns) and psychological (depression, anxiety, catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, alexithymia) domains. The review uses the biopsychosocial label descriptively but treats domains as parallel outcome categories without integration. Social domain is entirely absent. The review finds FM more severe than LBP in psychological distress and pain sensitivity, supporting a somatosensory continuum hypothesis. Methodological heterogeneity across 19 studies limits synthesis.
coding_rationale: BPS label used descriptively as 'biopsychosocial burden' without definition. Biological domain mentioned via central sensitization mechanisms. Psychological domain elaborated with 8 constructs. Social domain absent. Domains treated in parallel without integration. Typology: multifactorial. Integration: none proposed.

key_quotes_05_claim_verbatim: A diversity of methodological tools and measures used to assess the same pain-related, physiological and psychological outcomes was also revealed. This variety in methods, within subcategories such as anxiety, depression, pain sensitivity, and perceived disability, complicates comparability between studies and thus hinders the ability to synthesize findings across research.
key_quotes_05_why_it_matters: Highlights methodological heterogeneity as barrier to BPS integration
key_quotes_06_claim_verbatim: Many pain-related, physiological, and psychological similarities are shared between participants with FM and those with LBP. The main findings indicate that, across 19 studies, pain intensity, pain quality, quality of life, and kinesiophobia were frequently similar between the two conditions. However, FM appears more severe in pain catastrophizing, perceived disability, sensitivity to pain, anxiety and depression.
key_quotes_06_why_it_matters: Synthesizes key comparative findings across biological and psychological domains
